title: RBAC – Role‑Based Access Control 🔑
description: Define fine‑grained permissions with Roles and RoleBindings inside a namespace.

slides.title: The RBAC Rule Structure 📐
slides.content:
# A permission rule

Each rule in a Role specifies:
- **apiGroups** – which API group (e.g., `""` for core, `apps` for apps/v1)
- **resources** – object type (e.g., `pods`, `deployments`)
- **verbs** – actions allowed: `get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`

Example:
```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]          # core group
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
```

This allows reading Pods but not modifying them.

slides.title: Creating a Role YAML 📝
slides.content:
## A simple example

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: default
  name: pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
```

This Role exists only within the `default` namespace.

quizData.question: Where is a Role valid?

options.text: Only in the namespace where it is created

quizData.explanation: Roles are namespaced; ClusterRoles are cluster‑wide.

slides.title: RoleBinding – Granting the Role 🤝
slides.content:
## Link a subject to a Role

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: default
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: app-sa
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

Now the ServiceAccount `app-sa` can get/list/watch Pods in the `default` namespace.

slides.title: Test RBAC
slides.content: Use `kubectl auth can-i` to check access:

quizData.question: What does a RoleBinding do?

options.text: Grants the permissions in a Role to a subject
Defines a set of API rules

quizData.explanation: RoleBinding connects a Role to a user or ServiceAccount.

slides.title: Allowing Specific Resources by Name 🎯
slides.content:
## `resourceNames` for extra granularity

You can restrict access to individual objects:
```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  verbs: ["get"]
  resourceNames: ["my-secret"]
```

This grants read access only to the Secret named `my-secret`, not all secrets.

slides.title: Subresources (status, logs) 📊
slides.content:
## Access to specific sub‑resources

Some resources have sub‑resources like `pods/log` or `deployments/status`. You must explicitly list them:
```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
```

This allows reading logs but not the Pod itself.

quizData.question: True or False: A Role that allows `get pods` automatically allows `get pods/log`.
quizData.explanation: Logs are a separate subresource; you must explicitly grant access.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use `kubectl create role` and `kubectl create rolebinding` for imperative quick starts

```bash
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=default:app-sa
```

Then dump to YAML with `-o yaml --dry-run=client` for editing.
